doc.title: Holman Bill — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Wilfred Middlebrooks, Irv Cotler and Earl Palmer
summary: Short portraits of the bassist, Sinatra's favorite studio drummer, and Earl Palmer, who came in with rock and roll.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: You did reference your group with Mel Lewis. I‟m looking at a record date in May, Jazz for Five. That was the first time I saw Wilfred Middlebrooks listed as – credited on a session. So, could you talk about him? You just mentioned that he was the only bassist that would come out for after hours.

He didn‟t partake of the recording scene. The first time I met him was when we were looking for a player. But he was a good player. He should have been doing some other things. He later went with Ella Fitzgerald. Was with her for a long time. Later, Jimmy Rowles had to bow out, because he couldn‟t put up with the late night things, the sessions. So Lorraine Geller came on as the piano player. She was good too. It‟s Herb‟s wife.
Some of the other – as I mentioned earlier, some of the folks who didn‟t have as strong a reputation: drummer Irv Cotler. I saw him listed on a few dates. Any recollections?

He was an older guy. I don‟t know what bands he played with, but he was an accomplished studio player, mainly, and he was Sinatra‟s favorite drummer. Sinatra insisted on him all the time. I played very seldom – I think I made one record date that he was on. But I guess he was doing a lot of work. I‟m not sure.

Yeah, maybe because of some of your arranging credits, his name was listed in association with your name. Another drummer that came from New Orleans out here – I believe that you were on the scene when he arrived – Earl Palmer, who obviously got plenty of work in the studios.
Yeah. Earl came later. He wasn‟t in on the West Coast scene, that I know of. He came in with rock-and-roll. He was doing everything, and very well too.
